newsitem.title: USA: Sears earnings fall on costs for legal settlement.
newsitem.headline: Sears earnings fall on costs for legal settlement.

text.p: Sears, Roebuck and Co. said Thursday profits fell in the second quarter becase of a legal settlement with credit card customers, but its retailing business enjoyed strong results depite cool spring weather.

Sears, the nation's second-largest retailer, said profits fell 57 percent to $117 million, or 29 cents a share, in the second quarter compared with a year ago. Revenues rose to $9.7 billion from $9.1 billion in the second quarter of 1996.

This year's results included a $320 million charge for a previously announced settlement of class-action lawsuits and claims by attorneys general in 50 states that Sears was overly aggressive in collecting debt from credit card customers.
It also had a $126 million gain from an accounting change and the sale of its stake in data services business Advantis.

The charge was bigger than Wall Street anticipated and the largest taken since Chairman Arthur Martinez overhauled the retail business in 1993, closing 113 stores, chopping 50,000 jobs and shutting the storied Sears catalogue, resulting in a $1.7 billion charge.
The legal settlement overshadowed improvements in the retailing business, where results were better than expected.

"I look at this as a continuation of quarter-after-quarter of improved operating results," Martinez said in an interview. "Our focus is on the 16.5 percent increase" in net income excluding the extraordinary items.

Minus those items, earnings rose to $311 million, or 78 cents a share, in the second quarter from $274 million, or 67 cents a share, in the same period last year. Wall Street analysts had expected Sears to report earnings of just 74 cents a share, according to a survey by First Call.
Sears stock rose to a new 52-week high on the New York Stock Exchange to $58.69, up $2.19 in afternoon trading.

Retail sales were sluggish during the quarter because of chilly spring weather, which dampened demand for air conditioners and lawn and garden merchandise. Same-store sales, or sales of stores open at least a year, rose by 2.3 percent vs. 9.4 percent in the second quarter of 1996.

"The sales weren't strong, but profits were," said Michael Exstein of Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. Sears kept a tight rein on expenses, recorded higher profits in Canada and boosted results at its credit card operation despite higher delinquencies and personal bankruptcies.

While sales growth slowed, Sears still stole customers from competitors, including Montgomery Ward & Co. Inc., Martinez said. Sears has been considering acquiring between 10 and 50 stores from Montgomery Ward, the 408-store chain that filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection last week.
"There are a relatively modest number of stores that would be an interesting addition to our portfolio," he said.
Sears has been acquiring stores from weaker competitors and opening niche hardware, auto and furniture outlets in a drive to build its core retailing business.

Since 1992, it has shed almost all of its non-retailing businesses, including financial services company Dean Witter, Discover & Co. and insurer Allstate Corp. It sold its 30-percent stake in Advantis to International Business Machines Corp. for $450 million in June.
"Sears' massive deconglomeration has enabled the management to focus on the core Sears retail business," said Todd Slater of Lazard Freres & Co. Llc.

Sears' credit card business contributes about half of the company's annual profits. A big rise in personal bankruptcies and delinquencies by consumers has hurt credit card results of many retailers, and Sears has stepped up collection efforts and increased fees to help offset the setbacks.

Its aggressive collection efforts with consumers who had filed for personal bankruptcy got Sears in trouble. In June, it admitted it failed to properly file repayment agreements with those customers in bankruptcy court and agreed to a sweeping legal settlement.

The settlement cost more than anticipated because the company's original estimates did not include anticipated costs for a possible settlement with the U.S. Justice Department and for reimbursements for customers who entered repayments before 1992, analysts said.
